essay.q: Define algorithmic bias, and give one example from the lesson.
essay.model: Algorithmic bias is bias in AI judgments caused by bias in the training data. Example: a hiring AI that unfairly evaluates a particular gender, or a face-recognition AI that is more likely to misidentify particular ethnic groups.
points: Correct definition, linked to training data (1)
One of the book's two examples (1)

essay.q: What is meant by Moore's Law? Is it a fixed law of physics? Explain your answer.
essay.model: Moore's Law is the observation that the number of transistors on an integrated circuit doubles approximately every two years. It is not a fixed law of physics: it is an empirical observation of what has happened, and in recent years it has been said to be approaching a physical limit.
points: Transistors on an integrated circuit double (1)
Approximately every two years (1)
Not a law of physics — an empirical observation, said to be nearing a physical limit (1)
essay.src: p.5; p.8 Worked Example (2) A-B; ministry assessment, lesson 1

essay.q: Compare AR (augmented reality) and VR (virtual reality) in terms of what each one is and how it works.
essay.model: AR overlays digital information on real-world images, so the user still sees the real world with a digital layer added on top. VR immerses the user in a virtual space generated by a computer, replacing the real world with that space.
points: AR overlays digital information on real-world images (1)
VR immerses the user in a computer-generated virtual space (1)
The contrast: AR adds to the real world; VR replaces it (1)
essay.src: p.8 Worked Example (3); ministry assessment, lesson 1

essay.q: Spam filters and product recommendations are both examples of machine learning, but they do different tasks. Explain what they have in common, and why neither of them is generative AI.
essay.model: Both learn patterns from data and use those patterns to make predictions and judgments — that is what makes them machine learning. Neither is generative AI because neither produces new data: a spam filter sorts existing email, and a recommendation predicts an interest, whereas generative AI generates new text, images or audio.
points: Both learn patterns from data (1)
Both use them to make predictions or judgments (1)
Neither generates new data — they classify or predict (1)
essay.src: p.13 Think It Through; p.16 Try 2(2)

essay.q: A hospital wants to use image-diagnosis AI to detect diseases from X-ray images. Explain why the final diagnosis should be confirmed by a human doctor, referring to the black-box problem and to responsibility.
essay.model: The AI's decision-making process can be opaque — the black-box problem — so it is difficult to verify whether its result is correct. A wrong diagnosis can harm a patient, and final decision-making needs someone who is responsible for the result, which the AI cannot be. So a doctor should confirm it.
points: Black box: how the AI decided is unclear, so the result is hard to verify (1)
A wrong result can harm the patient (1)
Final decisions need a responsible human; the AI cannot be answerable (1)
essay.src: p.21 Think It Through; p.28 XAI and responsibility

essay.q: Analyze why AI is well suited to some tasks but requires caution in others. In your answer, refer to what AI is good at (finding patterns, recognition, prediction) and to what needs caution (ethical judgments, privacy, final decision-making).
essay.model: AI is well suited to tasks built on patterns in data: it can find and classify patterns in complex data such as images and text, recognise and generate images, audio and text, and make probabilistic predictions based on data — for example a recommendation system or image-diagnosis AI. It requires caution where those strengths stop being enough. Ethical judgments can lead to discrimination or prejudice, especially when the training data is biased, so they should not be left entirely to AI. Judgments involving personal information raise privacy issues. And final decision-making needs someone who is responsible for the result, while the AI's reasoning may be a black box. So AI is a powerful tool for pattern-based tasks, but human judgment is still needed for ethics, privacy and responsibility.
points: What AI is good at — patterns, recognition/generation, prediction — at least two (1)
Why: these tasks are based on patterns in data, with an example (1)
Ethical judgments: risk of discrimination or prejudice, linked to biased training data (1)
Privacy: judgments involving personal information (1)
Final decision-making: responsibility, and/or the black-box problem (1)
A conclusion that weighs the two sides — a tool for patterns, with human judgment kept for ethics, privacy and responsibility (1)
essay.marking: Six points, one mark each. A plain list of strengths and cautions with no reasoning earns no more than 3.
